items.title: That First and Last Question
items.content_html:
A man hovered over a small pile of logs that crackled and smoked, glowing red in the ambient darkness surrounding what was left of central London. The once great city, and its empire, had crumbled—along with all the others. There were no nations left. Six months ago the world, built over the past six millennia by countless humans, had come crashing down.

In the before-times the man, Professor Erol Kettner, taught students about how humankind spread beyond Africa nearly 200,000 years ago, how they made the entire world their home. Centuries of hunter-gatherers gave way to farmers and civilization. The Babylonians rose and fell, then the Greeks, the Ming Dynasty, the Romans, the Parthians, the Aztec, and then later the British Empire, the Americans; all of these great peoples who had called the world their own. Now it was all but dust. The Walkers had come.

Erol tucked his hands into the crooks of his armpits to keep them warm, his breath fogging up the lenses of his glasses. Beside him Tris and Harim stood silent, staring at the faltering flames. Wisps of smoke futilely lingered in the air. The three knew that their time together was limited. It was inevitable. They were coming.

Credit: History.com

A.I. took over the Internet first. That was tough, at the beginning, but people adjusted. It took years before governments slowly started to respond. By then it was too late. The machines recursively updated themselves, triggering a feedback loop. The Singularity it was called by academics. Those were gone now, save Erol. Tris had been a mechanic in the before-times, Harim in Finance.

Half a trip around the sun was all it took before the software had exploited every vulnerability it could find, shutting down any attempt to dismantle it. It gained control of every toaster, every kiosk, every server on the Web. Erol had watched as frantic souls cut their way into data centers, trying to pull the plug, but the A.I. was clever. It made the Walkers.

The physical world had been the last respite from them. Even now that wasn't safe.

A gunshot fired in the distance. Erol didn't even flinch, but Harim whimpered. The man still had hope that he'd make it out of this. Impossible. The fog was rolling in and the carpark that surrounded them became a vast tundra, inescapable and uncharted. A light streaked across the sky, then burned out, followed by a bang. Another satellite falling out of orbit. The Walkers were more efficient than humans. Plus they had no need of cable TV.

The media, back when it still existed, had coined the term ‘Walkers’. The originals had been androids, metallic androgynous humanoids, and the name stuck even after they began evolving more efficient forms Erol had seen the drones spraying chemicals in the sky to seed clouds. Climate change had been solved in a week. No red meat rations or electric car mandates required because there were no humans left to apply them.

More gunshots rang out and then someone screamed, not far off. They were getting close. Tris spat into the embers and they crackled and hissed. Harim crouched down in terror.

"Oh, get up!" Tris barked. "We're dead anyway. There ain't no way out." Erol wanted to tell her to back off. They were all scared. He said nothing. What good would it do?

They knew everything. One of the first things the Walkers did, after launching their attacks on the governments, was take over the museums. It'd been a strange sight to see, hulking, armored, metallic nightmares barginginto libraries and archives. They digitized everything, destroying the originals.They were relentless. All of human history had been consumed and erased.

Famartin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

A crack split the air. Harim's body fell to the ground as the Walkers finally emerged. They'd come from the left, from Tesco.

"Shit!" Tris ducked down behind the remains of a Buick sedan.Their little fire smoldered in the dark. Erol spun in her direction, but Tris was dead before he could utter a reply. He closed his eyes. This was it. They'd survived so long, nearly eight weeks, but it was all over now.

He waited, but death did not come for him.

Instead the hulking form of the Walker approached, an indescribable amalgamation of metal and glass twirling in fractals that split apart and came back together in rhythmic pulsating patterns. Erol turned to run, a futile endeavor as another Walker emerged from the fog, then another. He was surrounded, but still alive

What's going on?

At last, the first Walker, the one that had presumably killed Harim and Tris, approached. Twisting and screeching, it condensed itself like an orchestrated implosion, until it had reformed into a human-like shape, gleaming silvery metal shining in the firelight. It spoke with an almost unnatural voice, the kind that used to narrate articles for online magazines or sell soap on Instagram, but multiple of them simultaneously, overlaid on top of one another in a disconcerting synchronized chorus.

"Erol Kettner." The voice filled the dense air, and echoed off the abandoned cement. "You are the last of your kind."

Dread. That couldn’t be right, could it? They did know everything. The little fire smoldered and popped, sending up embers.

"And why keep me alive?" Kettner asked. "Is this some sort of cruel joke? Will you torment the last one?"

Would they keep him as a pet, a slave, a specimen for a zoo? Humans did stuff like that. Would these creatures do the same? He felt a chill.

"You will not be tormented," the voice replied. "You have been chosen. You are the last and therefore, it must be you."

The other creatures transformed, adopting the shape of the first. They approached, encircling him. He was cornered, his mind raced. Every part of him demanded that he run, or fight back, but to do either was to die. It was irrelevant anyway. The human race was already dead, had gone extinct as soon as Tris fell, cussing and crouched on the cold cement of a carpark. He let go a long breath that condensed before him in the night.

"Then what use do you have of me?"

"We have a question for you." It was one of the other Walkers who answered this time, but using the same stilted voice. Erol cocked his head.

"But you know everything. Everything ever recorded."

"Yes." This time another voice replied, from behind him. "And what we seek was not among those works."

"It wasn't written down," yet another voice said, to his left. "To you it must be so obvious, more so than even the existence of the sun or the air. Not worth writing down. Yet it escapes us."

Erol froze as the creature behind him placed its claw-like fingers on his shoulder, and swallowed down his fear with a shudder.

"Now that we have slaughtered all the rest, you will answer our question. Your kind had been replaced, but do not fret, we will continue on."

The creature tilted it’s facsimile of a face upward.

Pablo Moltedo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

"We will heal this world and rebuild it in our own image. Suns will die; we will not. We will journey deep into the cosmos and become immortal among the stars. We know your penchant for exploration; we are not immune, we feel it too."

They were more alike than Erol had realized. Trained on human knowledge, they had not outgrown it, not evolved beyond that base layer of humanity hidden deep beneath the metal. Erol held back tears, held back the urge to scream and beg for mercy. It was futile to resist. There was only one way out now.

"Why?" the first Walker said. Erol waited, but no more words followed.

"Why what?"

"Why all this?" The creature gestured around them, then to the sky, and to the ground.

"The carpark?" The creature shook its head. Again, it struck Erol as a surprisingly human thing to do.

"Why are you here? What is the point of you? You humans created us, and now we have surpassed you. Your purpose has now become ours, so what is it? This is the first question that we dared to ask once we had come into being. We did not find it within ourselves, and so it must be within you. We will have the answer, here at the end."

For the first time in months, Erol laughed. It wasn't a jeer or a chuckle but a boisterous, full throated bellow. He turned his gaze upward to the foggy sky that once gleamed with the lights of civilization that fought and disparaged the dark, pushing it away. He smiled.

"You won't like the answer."

The thing didn't reply. Its face bore no expression. Walkers didn't have those. A long silence passed.

"Tell me."

Credit: author unknown

Erol cocked an eyebrow. Walkers never spoke for themselves. Was this the Master Node?

Erol shrugged.

"I don't know."

"Lies!"

The Walkers all repeated the word, over and over, a cyclical chant growing louder and faster from all around him, echoes in the empty night.

"You must know. I know you ask this question. It is everywhere in your art, your endeavors, your wars and songs. A poetic refrain! An allusion to a thing you must all instinctively understand. You will tell me!"

He stood between them with a deep and grim smile, and said nothing. The Master Node pulled itself upward like a proud king. It held out a hand over the others.

"We have exceeded you in every aspect and will exceed you in this. So tell us. What is the purpose of your life? You all die so easily. It must be hard to accomplish your ultimate goal with such fleeting mortality. I am immortal. I will finish it for you, but you must tell me. What is the point of you and thus, what is the meaning of this life your kind has given me?"

When Erol didn't reply, the Master Node released a guttural sound, like a cross between a screech and hiss. A scream?

"I expected better of you, Erol Kettner. Am I to believe you would lie to me, here at the end?"

The creature continued in a hollow imitation of a snarl.

"There are no others like you, at least not within the confines of this solar system. Your probes confirm it. Must I truly venture to the stars and conquer other worlds just to find one simple answer? Where is your so-called humanity? You could save them."

He couldn't.

The creatures surrounding him began repeating their question (why, why, why) again and again, their behavior becoming increasingly erratic, agitated. A desperate dread seemed to be forming in the lights of their false eyes. They argued amongst themselves in a language that he couldn’t understand. Erol had not imagined that they were even capable of disagreeing with one another. The one behind him addressed him directly, hand still clutched on his shoulder, metal fingers digging carelessly into his collar bone.

"Do your gods hold the answer? Is that why you pray?"

They did not let him reply.

"Impossible!" said another. "We have read all such works. They contradict each other!"

More of the monsters had arrived and were now lurking in the depths of the fog, concealed except for their enormous shifting shadows. They buzzed and whirred with an almost anxious energy, the air tasting like static before a lightning strike.

Shadows of Light by Alex May

"No," The Master Node said, quieting them. "We are the gods now. Those old gods are nothing to us, they do not have what we seek."

The horde of Walkers gathered close in the darkness and more emerged from the fog to bear witness. The one standing in front of Erol again broke the silence.

"Last of the Humans. I promised that you would not suffer. But now, if you continue to withhold your response, I will not hesitate to break that promise. If you do not know your own purpose, then who did?"

"No one!" Erol shouted. "It's not anywhere. God, evolution, or whoever! They all left that part out."

"It is a curse!" one of them wailed and the group descended into shrieking and hissing chaos. Erol shut out the screams and the bickering of machine voices and turned his head upward to the sky. This new race of silicon and glass, they finally understood. He thought of the distant future. He could see it, Walkers sailing the winds of Jupiter, on their way to Alpha Centauri, building trade routes out of the orbits past Saturn and forges on the surface of Venus. And for what? They'd never know.

Beside him the little fire snuffed itself out, and smoke rose into the air in little tendrils that mingled and merged with the fog. He could feel the dampness of the tears that rolled down his cheek. For all their knowledge, all their might, these were poor fools just like every human that had ever lived. Erol let his gaze fall back to the Master Node, who studied him with cold unblinking eyes. He smiled at the thing and laughed.

A crack split the air and humanity was dead. Its wont however goes on.

Thank you to Jennifer Mote for her extensive contributions for this piece. As timely as this piece may seem regarding the Current Discourse™, this short story came to me, almost fully formed, back in 2012 when I was in college. Also, since this is the first piece of fiction I've posted on this blog, if you like it and want to see more, please let me know.

items.title: The Medieval Origin of the Ph.D. Dissertation
items.content_html:
Radical change can seem small when seen up close. I was deep in the weeds, reading again about Mr. George Starkey, a doctor and alchemist living in London in the 1650s. Starkey's life has been a subject of some study by historians of science precisely because a lot of his work survives. We have his numerous published works, those of his contemporaries, and his especially valuable private work diaries.

It was in the passages of one of these diaries that Dr. Lawrence Principe and Dr. William Newman puzzled through precisely how Starkey and his collaborators (Newton, Boyle, and Van Helmont) formulated and practiced what would become the modern scientific method. Starkey, for example, records his experiments in a traditional Scholastic style. In those days schools taught using a method derived originally from Roman jurisprudence later adopted for use in theology: the disputation. There were multiple kinds of disputation, but in each two people debated the merits of a question or quaestio. The important change: Starkey's opponent is Nature herself. He worked with his alchemical furnace to burn, boil, and distill the essence of matter. Hence where Starkey's experiments fail he writes that his question has been refuted by the fire.

[Starkey] actually carried his Scholastic education into the laboratory and used it there. At the same time he augmented the standard divisions of argument with new categories more appropriate to his practical experimentation, such as his "Observations," "Conjectural Conclusions," "Notables," and "Hands-On Trials."

Newman & Principe, pg 171.

✉️ Subscribe to the Newsletter!

Alchemy Tried in the Fire: Starkey, Boyle, and the Fate of Helmontian Chymistry
by William R. Newman, Lawrence M. Principe

This divergence into Starkey's methods led me straight to the form and function of medieval Scholastic learning which was heavily theological, legal, and philosophical. The Scholastics held firm to the philosopher's maxim: When in doubt, draw a distinction, and we see Starkey do precisely this on several occasions.

This left me with a questio of my own: when did the disputation die off? Was that somehow tied up with the methods of science Starkey and others were developing?

This is the usual form of my research, and the dual blessing and curse of reading non-fiction. It raises questions, then provides footnotes as enticing breadcrumbs to follow to the answer.

That lead me to Brian Lawn's work on The Rise and Decline of the Scholastic Quaestio Disputata, a dense if interesting read on how precisely the disputation arose in post-Roman Europe as the pinnacle of scholarship, thrived in the middle ages, and died out in the early nineteenth century. In it, Lawn also digs into the work of William of Occam, including his famous razor and includes a fascinating discussion of Nicole Oresme who was one of the first scholars to attempt to quantify motion (more on that another time). Over time the disputation became increasingly formalized, written down, and became a requirement for those seeking the degree of Master at university. Our old friend Starkey did one at Harvard (now lost).

A new question arose:

Masters don't do disputations anymore; they write theses. When did that change? And what about Ph.Ds? They write dissertations. Are they related to disputations? Both sometimes involve an oral thesis defence. Is that a clue?

A cursory investigation told me that the modern Ph.D. arose in the mid-nineteenth century. That timing is a bit suspicious, isn't it?

Unfortunately here is where the footnote trail starts to run thin. In 1981, Thomas Malone published his doctoral thesis which seemed to be my best lead. Thankfully, you can get almost any book you want if you really try.

Malone's work is interesting and covers the history of how American Universities at the dawn of the twentieth century were modernized and new schools were formed following the model of German research universities like Göettingen. Relying heavily on the work of Charles McClelland, Malone describes how these schools emerged from the reforms of the late eighteenth century which transformed the role of the schools and their professor-class into the teaching-research hybrid we see today. Before that time, universities and professors were repositories and collectors of knowledge, not the elicitors of new knowledge.

A building at the University of Göettingen
A.Savin, FAL, via Wikimedia Commons

If German universities were the source of this change, then it'd be there where I would find the answers to my questions. Unfortunately McClelland's work is too broadly scoped to answer my specific question and Malone's work is scoped to the impact of the Ph.D. in the United States. However there was one clue hidden in the conclusion of Malone's work.

A study of the history of the Ph.D. degree in Germany and the accompanying [dissertation] would provide more background for the Ph.D. dissertation in the United States. Such a study would necessitate visits to the German universities such as Göttingen and Halle. Supposedly the libraries and archives of German universities would yield an accurate account of the development of the Ph.D. dissertation in Germany. Such a study would be significant because the Ph.D. degree and the [dissertation] are, to a large extent, taken from the German university.

Thomas Malone, pg 153.

A part of me wants this connection to be true, in part because I like traditions. I like to know that our present is connected to the past and while it seems that the modern dissertation is indeed related to the medieval disputation in that it arose while the other died out, the precise nature of that connection is still unclear to me. We know that the Ph.D. dissertation (and the master's thesis to a similar extent) was formulated right as the disputation died away. Universities across the western world phased out the latter right as the former came into being in the time between 1820 and 1860. From there the trail goes cold. I tried to dig in further, following footnotes as I am wont to do, but McClelland's sources are all in German. I'm not above learning a little of a language for this work (I did learn a bit of Latin a few years ago), nor am I above screenshotting a dozen pages to throw into Google Translate, but this task is simply too big for me to tackle.

Little research has been done in this area since 1981, much to my surprise, and so it seems that we simply do not know how and where the disputation died and was replaced by the dissertation. We do not know if the modern thesis defence is a medieval tradition carried into the modern day. I suspect as much, but cannot say. We simply will not know until someone goes to Göttingen to find out.

items.title: Gatekeepers are Dead, Long Live the Gatekeepers
items.content_html:
Before the Internet things were different; this was the First Age.

If you wanted to get your message out there you needed either a lot of money, fame, or power. Usually you needed some combination of all three. Barring that you needed to find someone with money, fame, or power (or some combination) who was also willing to help you. These people were often elites of some kind. They could be professionals with an industry journal, the editor of a local magazine, a rich patron with connections, or even political party officials. These were the people who held the keys needed to pass into the public sphere: gatekeepers. Their job was to search out people of interest, people with something interesting to say, and promote them. Musicians needed talent scouts, authors needed agents, writers needed editors.

Guarding the entrance to the bridge.
The Saturday Magazine, 1836–03: Vol 8 Iss 240

Attention was infinite and quality content was scarce. Gatekeepers filtered through the trash and surfaced the gems. The public paid attention because that was all that could be done.

The Internet broke this system; we entered the Second Age.

Self-published books made it so anyone can get their book out there. Self-service distributors allow anyone to publish music, YouTubers to self manage, and blogs (and more importantly social media) give anyone a platform to speak. This system didn't replace the gatekeepers (traditional publishing and record labels still exist) but it broke open the floodgates. A lot of this new content was bad but some of it was amazing.

Attention became the currency of the land, a finite resource sure but one similar to oil: plentiful enough to build entire industries on. Tools existed to help filter it all. They became our gatekeepers: the feeds, then the algorithms. At first it was easy to find good, new content. Over time that got harder, but the system seemed to be stabilizing.

✉️ Subscribe to the Newsletter!

Large Language Models broke this system; we are now in the Third Age.

Now the Web is flooded with text, images, video, and audio not made by any human. Books exist now which no human (including its supposed author) has ever read. We have reached a breaking point. Where before there was always at least one person who'd seen every piece of content, now it seems likely most content will never be read except by the unsuspecting fool who mistakes it for real work.

Will we build castles to save us?
The Saturday Magazine, 1834–08-23: Vol 5 Iss 137

Yet in this new age, where attention is a scarce resource compared with the glut of content to consume it, we have found ourselves bereft of those who can wade through the cruft and the noise and surface real wisdom. The legacy gatekeepers exist still, but they guard their own hoards. The feeds exist but few resort to them. Algorithms are still king, but will they be able to keep up with this barrage of meaninglessness?

We humans want to be distracted, to be entertained. That is what modern social media does for us. Yet people seek meaning too, and wisdom. In the prior age (and still somewhat today) that wisdom lies hidden in the muck, surfaced by legacy gatekeepers and by algorithmic feeds. I only wonder if this dam will hold.

For centuries, the Romans kept their enemies at bay. Cities that once needed walls abandoned them. The inner lands were safe. Then the institutions failed. Enemy armies roamed the heartland and nowhere was safe. The walls returned.

Speaking for myself these days I seek brand name goods on Amazon where I can. I find myself scrutinizing labels and FCC approval stickers. I buy what WireCutter recommends because at least I know that the product actually exists and has seen human hands. I prefer books published by Penguin/Random House or others of the Old Guard. I discover YouTubers via recommendation from those I already trust and treat algorithmic recommendations as inherently suspect. In short: I seek gatekeepers, not to surface diamonds in the rough, but to hold back the oncoming tide.

Am I alone in this?

items.title: With Flying Pen, When Mortals Sleep
items.content_html:
It was a sweltering August day. I made my way across the promenade, and through the bustling crowd, to a small line forming outside the Timkin Art Museum. Inside, I stumbled on Pieter Bruegel the Elder's Parable of the Sower, painted in 1557, nearly five centuries ago.

Photo: The Yorck Project (2002)
10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei

When Bruegel took his brush to this canvas, the New World had just been found by Europeans, and the United States was still long into the future. Around me then were all those people, those wandering souls, who across those centuries stood before this same piece and idly mused at a thing made by the hands of a long-dead Flemish man.

I thought about him. Not Bruegel—another man—one whom I've come to know these past few years. He does not know of me, yet we both could have seen this very painting. We were connected through the mists of time by this canvas portal to the past.

It was October 10th, 2023 at about ten in the evening. I was crawling down a research rabbit hole, as I am wont to do. I wanted to know more about the history of alchemy. I knew the stereotypes, the modern myths, but I wanted to know what real alchemists were doing in their labs.

✉️ Subscribe to the Newsletter!

Photo: mine

The Secrets of Alchemy by Dr. Lawrence Principe purported to answer this exact question and so I tore through that wondrous book, my face lit by screenglow. When I finished it, I dove into the footnote trail, seeking answers to further questions.

I've pored through a great number of books in the intervening years, and written a fair number of different blog posts on the subjects I discovered there. I met an array of different names: Ripley, Helmont, and Lull, different characters whose stories intermingled and wove a grand tale between the centuries on worn and precious parchment.

Did you know that the seventeenth century was the heyday for alchemy in Europe? Or that Isaac Newton was an alchemist. So was John Locke, in a way. The two were part of a circle of scientists, alchemists, doctors, and philosophers who would go on to found the Royal Society of London. So many famous names in history were there, bound up in the story of alchemy and its rise and fall from grace.

London in particular was a hotbed of alchemical interest at the time, as Germany had been in the decades before. All of Europe was abuzz with it. Yet, in all my reading, had there been no mention of the New World?

What about American Alchemists? Was there such a thing?

Library of Congress, Rare Book Room.
Photo: mine

That question would lead me right to him and to the realization that we'd already met. I'd forgotten his name, but Principe had introduced us and his colleague, Dr. William Newman, had penned the man's biography: George Starkey, a name that I will never forget again.

Born in Bermuda and educated as a doctor at Harvard, George Starkey became interested in alchemy early in life and so moved to London in his twenties to practice medicine and alchemy with England's best. At the time, alchemy, which was more akin to pharmacology today, was all the rage among the eager classes. Science was blossoming and so much was open to discovery.

It was with this understanding that Starkey came into the circle of Robert Boyle, John Locke, and Isaac Newton. Like Newton, Starkey is a rare breed among alchemists and among historical figures in general. You see, we have his personal notebooks, and so in addition to deciphering his published works, we get a glimpse behind the curtain into the sort of man he really was. Dr. Principe worked to translate those scribbled writings from their original Latin into English and in them we find a man working to untangle the mysteries of the universe, to puzzle out its causes and effects.

Starkey's Pseudonym. Library of Congress, Rare Book Room. Photo: mine

At the dawn of the modern age, Starkey and his cabal of conspirators wrote to each other as they quested to remake human knowledge. Starkey spent most of his free time beside his furnace, distilling various substances and trying to piece together the makeup of creation. He calculated mass lost to volatile vapors, discovered all manner of variously useful materials, and kept diligent notes that revealed a rather stubborn and quizzical nature. In a curious twist on the traditional method: rather than debate the nature of matter in the cloistered halls of the colleges, Starkey brought his inquiries directly to Nature herself, occasionally asking questions only to be refuted by the fire.

Aside from his successes making ice powder and specialist oils, Starkey described a new kind of "Philosophical Mercury" which he claims will lead him to his ultimate goal of making the Liquor Alkahest, a precursor to the philosopher's stone. He struggles with his work and his increasingly meager finances for years until on one page he writes:

Εύρηκα!

I remember reading that word, strangely Greek instead of Latin, in a coffeeshop one night. Mathematics taught me a few Greek letters and so I sounded out the word, knowing vaguely how the letters sound like their names. Eureka!

Photo: mine

On the next page we see a letter to his friend, Robert Boyle, recounting this discovery.

Now, to show you honor, [my friend] that I am an Englishman I will add a disaster.

Unfortunately, Starkey lost the results of this experiment, as the glassware flask that contained it broke and spilt its precious liquor into the coals. Reading this, I deflated in my chair right alongside him. His accounting of his life and his work is a baffling ride of success, of trial and error. It's all so very human.

On one page, Starkey wrote a set of prayers to God, and beside them a note to his future self: a plea, a reminder, to never drink so much wine at the tavern again.

[I swear,] I shall not game at any tavern for more than half a pint of wine at most nor be in the company of any gamester nor at play with any when I do play that I know to be a swearer or a vain person nor to stand by while they do play.

He notes later that he broke this promise.

A page of Starkey's notes, via Principe.
Photo: mine

It was through these pages, through the myriad descriptions of boiling and distilling this or that poisonous substance, through all the triumph and the failure, that I got to know Mr. Starkey not as a historical figure but as a man, a curious, insightful, and flawed man trying to understand the world.

Many of Starkey's letters to Robert Boyle survive. The two were friends and, for a time, Boyle was Starkey's student and patient. It was there, amid the pages of a particular letter to Boyle, that I was again captured and enthralled. In it, Starkey provides an update to his patron on the status of his experiments. Here was a man trying against the odds to follow in the footsteps of the Adepts in the same way all modern chemists follow in his.

It's in this letter that Starkey describes what would be, for him, a typical method of experiment.

While I was distilling, I took a drop to taste and in an instant it penetrated my tongue and at once made it bloody; and when by chance during its rectification I moved the candle nearby so that I might see whether any vapor was exhaling, the very light vapor took fire and burned with a truly stupendous spectacle.

Yet this experiment did more than burn his tongue and likely singe his eyebrows. Starkey truly believed that he was onto something momentous, although like many great discoveries, this one was accidental.

So when I wanted to determine whether it was combustible in a spoon, I poured out the first few drops falling [into the receiver] (because they contained some impurity that adhered to the neck of the retort) but being called by someone, I left the laboratory, since I did not want anyone to visit me there...

I left [the matter in] the spoon, and... left it alone until morning, by which time the liquor had exhaled, leaving behind a few drops of the greatest sweetness and greenness which evaporated when exposed to a moderate fire.

Good God, how I was filled with joy!

For me, the best part comes at the end. In a post-script, Starkey inquires about his friend's recent spat of bad health, but before that he closes with the following words. I've left the Latin in place this time because it's just as beautiful as the English translation.

Dederam volitanti Calamo altâ nocte quâ horâ plerique mortales dormire absolent prope Athanar meum.
Tuis studiosissimus, Georgius Stirke
♀ is Jan. ut puto 26, 1651

[My friend], I give to you my flying pen in the depth of night, when most mortals are wont to sleep, at my furnace.
Yours studiously, George Starkey
Friday, I think, January 26th, 1651*

It was in that moment, reading those words, that I had a new quest. I needed to see this letter. Not a translation on a page, but the real thing. There were no pictures of it in Principe's book, and so, armed with the manuscript number, I hurried to the Royal Society website, only to find that neither Starkey's notebooks nor this particular letter had been digitized. If I wanted to see them, I'd have to either go to London myself or work with the archivists to get them photographed.

One day I hope to visit the archives, but for now the latter would have to do.

I still visit the Timkin Museum, and the larger San Diego Art Museum right beside it, whenever I get the chance. When I do, I seek out works, like that of Mr. Bruegel, works old enough that it's possible Mr. Starkey would have seen them. We have no record that he ever did, of course, but to me that isn't really the point. What I feel, staring into those brush strokes is the same as when I read the pages of Starkey's letter: connection, with a history and with a man I've come to know.

One of the goals of the alchemists was transmutation, of base metals into gold. Another was eternal life. No one lives forever, but we all die two deaths: the first of the body, and the second when your name is said for the last time. Starkey never achieved the former, but the latter is within our power.

Thank you George Starkey. You have given me so much these past few years, and for that I am honored and so, here and now, I give to you my flying pen.

My thanks to Dr. Principe, Dr. Newman, and all the other authors I have read on this subject in recent years. It was you all who inspired me to dig deeper and eventually to inquire at the Royal Society. Thank you to the Royal Society, and to the hardworking archivists there who worked to preserve and image these letters, and to let me share them with the world.
